text: The Encyclopædia Britannica, meaning 'British Encyclopaedia' in Latin, is a general-knowledge English-language encyclopaedia first published between 1768 and 1771 in Edinburgh, Scotland, in weekly instalments that combined into three volumes. It has been published continuously since 1768 and is currently owned by Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc. The 2010 version of the 15th edition, spanning 32 volumes and 32,640 pages, was the last printed edition. Since 2016, it has been published exclusively online at Britannica.com. Printed for 245 years, it was the longest-running in-print encyclopaedia in the English language. The second edition expanded to 10 volumes, and by its fourth edition (1801–1810), it had grown to 20 volumes. Since the beginning of the 20th century, its total word count has remained roughly steady at about 40 million words. The 9th (1875–1889) and 11th (1911) editions are recognized as landmark works for scholarship and literary style. Starting with the 11th edition, after acquisition by an American firm, articles were shortened and simplified to appeal to the North American market. Though published in the United States since 1901, the Britannica has maintained British English spelling. In 1932, it adopted a policy of "continuous revision," updating articles on a schedule, a practice pioneered by Compton's Pictured Encyclopedia. The 15th edition (1974–2010) has a three-part structure: a 12-volume Micropædia of short articles (generally fewer than 750 words), a 17-volume Macropædia of long articles (two to 310 pages), and a single Propædia volume providing a hierarchical outline of knowledge. The Micropædia serves for quick fact-checking and as a guide to the Macropædia, with readers advised to study the Propædia to understand a subject's context and locate more detailed articles. The Britannica faced strong competition from digital encyclopaedias such as Microsoft Encarta and Wikipedia, and despite its reputation for authoritative, comprehensive, structured, and scholarly content, it could not match their breadth of coverage or continuous updating. In March 2012, it announced it would cease printing and focus solely on the online version. Past owners include Colin Macfarquhar and Andrew Bell, Archibald Constable, A. & C. Black, Horace Everett Hooper, Sears Roebuck, William Benton, and Jacqui Safra. Recent advances in information technology and the rise of electronic encyclopaedias reduced demand for print editions. To remain competitive, Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc. emphasized its reputation, reduced prices and production costs, and developed electronic versions on CD-ROM, DVD, and the web, while also promoting spin-off reference works. The Britannica has been issued in 15 editions, with multi-volume supplements to the 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th editions, and the 5th and 6th editions were reprints of the 4th. The 10th edition was a supplement to the 9th, and the 12th and 13th editions were supplements to the 11th. For the 15th edition (1974), the Britannica underwent a massive reorganization and became the New Encyclopædia Britannica. The 14th and 15th editions were edited annually, so later printings differed significantly from early ones. Throughout its history, the Britannica has aimed to be an excellent reference book and to provide educational material; in 1974, it adopted a third goal: to systematize all human knowledge. Its history is divided into five eras. The first era (1st–6th editions, 1768–1824) was managed by its founders, Colin Macfarquhar and Andrew Bell, Archibald Constable, and others. The first edition was compiled by William Smellie, with minor help from James Anderson, and included articles and longer "treatises" in a single alphabetical sequence, a structure inspired by Dennis de Coetlogon's Universal History of Arts and Sciences. The early Britannica, though compiled by Scots and using Scottish sources, was not widely recognized by participants in the Scottish Enlightenment and was not titled the Encyclopaedia Scotorum; by the third edition, it had evolved into a symbol of Britishness. During the second era (7th–9th editions, 1827–1901), managed by A & C Black, the Britannica included a general index for the first time in the 7th edition, a practice maintained until 1974. The 9th edition, edited by Thomas Spencer Baynes, was dubbed the "Scholar's Edition" and is the most scholarly of all Britannicas, with William Robertson Smith assisting after 1880; no biographies of living persons were included, and James Clerk Maxwell and Thomas Huxley served as special science advisors. By the end of the 19th century, the 9th edition was outdated and the Britannica faced financial difficulties. In the third era (10th–14th editions, 1901–1973), American businessmen introduced direct marketing and door-to-door sales, simplifying articles for a mass market. The 10th edition was an eleven-volume supplement to the 9th, while the 11th edition was a completely new work, heavily developed by Horace Hooper. After Hooper's financial troubles, Sears Roebuck managed the Britannica from 1920–1923 and 1928–1943. In 1932, Elkan Harrison Powell, vice-president of Sears, became president and initiated the policy of continuous revision. In 1943, Sears donated the Britannica to the University of Chicago, with William Benton providing working capital; Benton became chairman and managed the Britannica until his death in 1973. He established the Benton Foundation, which managed the Britannica until 1996, with the University of Chicago as the sole beneficiary. In 1974, the 15th edition was introduced under Mortimer J. Adler, who was a member of the Board of Editors since 1949 and chair from 1974, and director of editorial planning for the 15th edition from 1965. The 15th edition aimed to be a good reference work, educational tool, and to systematize all human knowledge. The initial version lacked a separate index and grouped articles into parallel encyclopaedias (Micropædia and Macropædia), provoking criticism, leading to a complete reorganization and indexing for a 1985 re-release. This second version continued through the 2010 print edition, officially titled The New Encyclopædia Britannica, also promoted as Britannica 3. On 9 March 1976, the US Federal Trade Commission issued an order prohibiting deceptive advertising and sales practices by Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc. In the fourth era (1974–1994), the 15th edition was reorganized into three parts: the Micropædia, Macropædia, and Propædia. From 1985, the Britannica consisted of four parts: the Micropædia, Macropædia, Propædia, and a two-volume index. The 2007 Macropædia contains 699 in-depth articles, ranging from two pages to 310 pages, with references and named contributors; the 2007 Micropædia contains roughly 65,000 articles, with about 97% under 750 words, no references, and no named contributors. The Micropædia is for quick fact-checking and guiding readers to the Macropædia; the Macropædia provides authoritative commentaries and stores information not covered elsewhere. The longest article (310 pages) is on the United States, resulting from merging articles on individual states. A 2013 "Global Edition" contains approximately 40,000 articles. The Britannica was dedicated to the British monarch from 1788 to 1901, then to both the British monarch and the President of the United States; the 11th edition is dedicated to King George V and President William Howard Taft, and the 1954 14th edition to President Dwight D. Eisenhower and Queen Elizabeth II, reflecting shifts in the relative power and sales of the two English-speaking nations. The final print edition was in 2010, a 32-volume set. The Britannica Global Edition, also printed in 2010, contains 30 volumes and 18,251 pages, with 8,500 photographs, maps, flags, and illustrations, and over 40,000 articles written by scholars worldwide, including Nobel Prize winners. Unlike the 15th edition, it does not contain Macro- or Micropædia sections and runs A through Z as earlier editions did. In 2020, Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc. released the Britannica All New Children's Encyclopedia: What We Know and What We Don't, the first children's encyclopaedia since 1984, widely praised for bringing back print.

The Encyclopædia Britannica's content is divided into the Micro- and Macropædia, comprising 12 and 17 volumes respectively, each with roughly one thousand pages. The 2007 Macropædia contains 699 in-depth articles, ranging from two to 310 pages, including references and named contributors, while the 2007 Micropædia has approximately 65,000 articles, about 97% of which are under 750 words, lack references, and have no named contributors. Micropædia articles are designed for quick fact-checking and to guide users to more detailed Macropædia entries, whereas Macropædia articles serve as authoritative commentaries and repositories of information not covered elsewhere. The longest article, 310 pages long, covers the United States, formed by merging entries on individual U.S. states. A 2013 "Global Edition" includes about 40,000 articles. Information is accessed via cross-references in the Micropædia and Macropædia, which average one per page, or through the alphabetical index or the Propædia, which organizes content by topic. The Propædia's core is the "Outline of Knowledge," a logical framework used by editors to select articles for inclusion and as a study guide, though libraries rarely use it and reviewers have recommended its removal. The Propædia includes color transparencies of human anatomy and appendices listing staff, advisors, and contributors. Together, the Micropædia and Macropædia contain roughly 40 million words and 24,000 images. The two-volume index has 2,350 pages, listing 228,274 topics and 474,675 subentries. The Britannica generally uses British spelling, such as colour (not color), centre (not center), and encyclopaedia (not encyclopedia), with exceptions like defense (not defence), and alternative spellings are cross-referenced (e.g., "Color: see Colour"). Since 1936, at least 10% of articles are revised annually; in the 2007 edition, 46% were revised over three years according to one source, while another reports 35%. Articles in the Micropædia and Macropædia are alphabetized with diacritical marks and non-English letters ignored, numerical entries like "1812, War of" treated as "Eighteen-twelve, War of," and articles with identical names ordered by person, place, then thing; rulers with identical names are ordered by country then chronology (e.g., Charles III of France before Charles I of England), and places with shared names are ordered by country then by smaller political divisions. In March 2012, the company announced the 2010 edition would be the last printed version, part of a shift to digital distribution; the peak print year was 1990, when 120,000 sets were sold, dropping to 40,000 annually by 1996; 12,000 sets of the 2010 edition were printed, with 8,000 sold by March 2012, and the remaining copies sold out by late April 2012. As of 2016, a replica of the 1768 first edition is available online. Britannica Junior was first published in 1934 as 12 volumes, expanded to 15 in 1947 and renamed Britannica Junior Encyclopædia in 1963, then discontinued after the 1984 printing. A British Children's Britannica edited by John Armitage was issued in London in 1960, with content based largely on the eleven-plus tests; it was introduced to the U.S. market in 1988 for ages seven to 14. In 1961, a 16-volume Young Children's Encyclopaedia was released for early readers; My First Britannica targets ages six to 12, and the Britannica Discovery Library serves children aged three to six (1974–1991). Compton's by Britannica, first published in 2007, combines the former Compton's Encyclopedia and includes 26 volumes and 11,000 pages, aimed at 10- to 17-year-olds. Abridged editions exist, such as the single-volume Britannica Concise Encyclopædia with 28,000 short articles condensing the 32-volume set; authorized translations are available in Chinese (by Encyclopedia of China Publishing House) and Vietnamese. Since 1938, an annual Book of the Year has been published to update the encyclopaedia, named by publication year but covering the previous year's events and statistics. Specialized works include Shakespeare: The Essential Guide to the Life and Works of the Bard (2006). The Britannica Ultimate Reference Suite 2012 DVD contains over 100,000 articles, including content from the Student and Elementary Encyclopaedias, with supplementary materials like maps, videos, sound clips, animations, and web links, plus study tools and Merriam-Webster dictionary and thesaurus entries. Britannica Online features over 120,000 articles, updated regularly, with daily features and links to The New York Times and BBC; as of 2009, about 60% of revenue came from online operations, with 15% from consumer subscriptions (available yearly, monthly, or weekly), and institutional subscriptions being a key part of the business. Starting in early 2007, articles are freely accessible if hyperlinked from external sites; non-subscribers see pop-ups and ads. On 20 February 2007, Britannica partnered with AskMeNow to launch a mobile encyclopaedia allowing text-message queries with answers from the 28,000-article concise edition and daily features. On 3 June 2008, a collaboration initiative between online experts and amateurs with editorial oversight was announced, with approved contributions credited but granting Britannica perpetual, irrevocable rights. On 22 January 2009, president Jorge Cauz announced public edits to the online Britannica would be accepted, requiring real-name registration, with all edits reviewed and approved by staff; user content would be separated from expert content and appear in a distinct section with a "Britannica Checked" stamp. On 14 September 2010, Britannica partnered with Concentric Sky to launch iPhone products for K–12; on 20 July 2011, the Britannica Kids line was ported to Intel Atom-based Netbooks, and on 26 October 2011, an iPad app was launched. In 2010, Britannica ImageQuest was released as an image database. In March 2012, printing was discontinued in favor of digital distribution. On 7 June 2018, Britannica released a Google Chrome extension, "Britannica Insights," showing Britannica snippets during Google searches, also available as a Firefox extension (later removed due to a code review). The print edition has 4,411 contributors, many eminent, such as Milton Friedman, Carl Sagan, and Michael DeBakey; roughly a quarter are deceased (some as early as 1947, e.g., Alfred North Whitehead), another quarter are retired or emeritus; about 98% contribute to only one article, with 64 to three, 23 to four, 10 to five, and 8 to more than five; Christine Sutton of Oxford contributed 24 articles on particle physics. Notable authors include Albert Einstein, Marie Curie, Leon Trotsky, and Isaac Asimov, though some have been criticized for lacking expertise; in 1911, historian George L. Burr criticized a contributor for lacking authority and called it "Americanizing." As of 2007, Dale Hoiberg, a sinologist, was Senior Vice President and editor-in-chief; predecessors include Hugh Chisholm (1902–1924), James Louis Garvin (1926–1932), Franklin Henry Hooper (1932–1938), Walter Yust (1938–1960), Harry Ashmore (1960–1963), Warren E. Preece (1964–1968, 1969–1975), Sir William Haley (1968–1969), Philip W. Goetz (1979–1991), and Robert McHenry (1992–1997). Anita Wolff was Deputy Editor and Theodore Pappas Executive Editor; prior Executive Editors include John V. Dodge (1950–1964) and Philip W. Goetz. Paul T. Armstrong is the longest-serving employee, having worked from 1934 to 1992, holding positions including treasurer, vice president, and chief financial officer. The 2007 editorial staff included five Senior Editors and nine Associate Editors, supervised by Dale Hoiberg and four others, who helped write Micropædia articles and some Macropædia sections. As of 2012, Britannica had an editorial board of advisors, primarily scholars. The Propædia and its Outline of Knowledge were developed by dozens of advisors under Mortimer J. Adler; roughly half have since died, including Rene Dubos (d. 1982), Loren Eiseley (d. 1977), Harold D. Lasswell (d. 1978), Mark Van Doren (d. 1972), Peter Ritchie Calder (d. 1982), and Mortimer J. Adler (d. 2001); the Propædia also lists nearly 4,000 advisors consulted for unsigned Micropædia articles. From 1974, the company was controlled by the Benton Foundation, with the University of Chicago as sole beneficiary; in January 1996, it was purchased by billionaire Swiss financier Jacqui Safra, who is current chair of the board; Don Yannias became CEO in 1997. In 1999, Britannica.com Incorporated was created to develop digital versions; Yannias became CEO of the new company, with his parent role vacant for two years; his tenure was marked by missteps, layoffs, and financial losses. In 2001, Yannias was replaced by Ilan Yeshua, who reunited the two companies; Yannias later returned to investment management and remains on the board. In 2003, Jorge Aguilar-Cauz was appointed President of Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc., reporting directly to the board and pursuing brand alliances and new educational products, continuing a strategy from former CEO Elkan Harrison Powell. A new subsidiary company, Britannica.com Incorporated, was created to develop digital versions of the Britannica; Yannias became CEO of the new company, while his former position at the parent company remained vacant for two years. Yannias' tenure at Britannica.com Incorporated was marked by missteps, significant layoffs, and financial losses. In 2001, Yannias was replaced by Ilan Yeshua, who reunited the leadership of the two companies. Yannias later returned to investment management but remains on Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc.'s Board of Directors. In 2003, Jorge Aguilar-Cauz, a former management consultant, was appointed President of Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc., serving as the senior executive who reports directly to the Board of Directors. Cauz has pursued alliances with other companies and extended the Britannica brand to new educational and reference products, continuing the strategy initiated by former CEO Elkan Harrison Powell in the mid-1930s. Prior to 1920, the Britannica was primarily sold by mail-order; after that time, it was almost exclusively sold by door-to-door salesmen, who often used high-pressure sales tactics or outright deception to secure purchases of the expensive work, earning a commission of $120–200 (approximately $932–$1,553 adjusted for inflation) in the United States in 1971. These tactics led to high turnover among salesmen, with the company exaggerating the ease of making a sale to employees and engaging in deceptive job advertising to attract recruits. The Britannica was sued several times by the American Federal Trade Commission for deceptive practices, a pattern common among American encyclopaedia companies. The significant sales force began developing in 1932, and by the late 20th century, most senior leadership came from the sales division. Early on, the Britannica was marketed to adults, especially an elite educated audience, but by the mid-20th century, it was primarily marketed to middle-class parents seeking a good education for their children, despite the content not being suitable for children's reading levels. The Britannica differentiated itself from other encyclopaedias by leveraging its long history to establish a premium brand image. Once purchased, the encyclopaedia was typically opened only a few times a year by an average owner. As a general encyclopaedia, it does not compete with specialized works such as the Encyclopaedia of Mathematics or the Dictionary of the Middle Ages, which focus more deeply on specific topics. In its early years, its main competitors were Ephraim Chambers' general encyclopaedia, Rees's Cyclopædia, and Coleridge's Encyclopædia Metropolitana; in the 20th century, competitors included Collier's Encyclopedia, the Encyclopedia Americana, and the World Book Encyclopedia. From the 9th edition onward, the Britannica was widely regarded as having the greatest authority among general English-language encyclopaedias, especially due to its broad coverage and eminent authors, and its print version was significantly more expensive than its competitors. Since the early 1990s, the Britannica has faced challenges from digital information sources, particularly the Internet, which has become a common and accessible source of information, enabled by search engines and initiatives like Google Books, MIT's educational materials, and the open PubMed Central library. The Internet provides more current coverage than print media because content can be updated easily and made available quickly, especially in rapidly changing fields such as science, technology, politics, culture, and modern history, where the Britannica has struggled to stay current—a problem first systematically analyzed by former editor Walter Yust. As a result, the Britannica shifted its focus to its online edition. The Britannica has been compared to other print encyclopaedias both qualitatively and quantitatively; Kenneth Kister conducted a comparison of the 1993 Britannica with Collier's Encyclopedia and the Encyclopedia Americana, selecting ten articles at random—circumcision, Charles Drew, Galileo, Philip Glass, heart disease, IQ, panda bear, sexual harassment, Shroud of Turin, and Uzbekistan—and assigning letter grades of A–D or F in four categories: coverage, accuracy, clarity, and recency. In all categories, the average grades for all three encyclopaedias fell between B− and B+, largely because none of the encyclopaedias had an article on sexual harassment in 1994. In accuracy, the Britannica received one "D" and seven "A"s, Encyclopedia Americana received eight "A"s, and Collier's received one "D" and seven "A"s; thus, the Britannica averaged 92% accuracy, compared to Americana's 95% and Collier's 92%. In timeliness, the Britannica averaged 86%, compared to Americana's 90% and Collier's 85%. The most notable competitor among CD/DVD-ROM digital encyclopaedias was Encarta, now discontinued, which incorporated three print encyclopaedias—Funk & Wagnalls, Collier's, and the New Merit Scholar's Encyclopedia—and was the top-selling multimedia encyclopaedia in the United States from January 2000 to February 2006. Both the digital Britannica and Encarta occupied a similar price range: the 2007 Encyclopædia Britannica Ultimate CD or DVD cost US$40–50, while the Microsoft Encarta Premium 2007 DVD cost US$45. The Britannica disc contains 100,000 articles and Merriam-Webster's Dictionary and Thesaurus (US only), offering primary and secondary school editions. Encarta contained 66,000 articles, a user-friendly Visual Browser, interactive maps, math, language, and homework tools, a US and UK dictionary, and a youth edition. Like the Britannica, Encarta was available online by subscription, though some content was free. Both digital encyclopaedias have been criticized for favoring U.S. audiences; the Britannica has less frequently updated UK-related articles, more detailed U.S. maps than those of other countries, and lacks a UK dictionary. The main online alternative to Britannica is Wikipedia. Key differences include accessibility, participation models, editorial policies, age, scope, language availability, and economic models: unlike Britannica, Wikipedia is not-for-profit, does not carry advertising, and is not connected to traditional publishing distribution networks. Britannica articles either have known authorship or a set of possible authors (the editorial staff); with the exception of the editorial staff, most contributors are experts in their field, some of whom are Nobel laureates. In contrast, Wikipedia articles are typically written by individuals of unknown expertise, many of whom are anonymous and lack verifiable credentials. Former Britannica editor-in-chief Robert McHenry noted in 2004 that Wikipedia could not hope to rival Britannica in accuracy due to the lack of institutional vetting. In 2005, the journal Nature compared science articles from both websites to field experts for peer review, receiving 42 usable reviews. The study found eight serious errors—four from each site—and numerous factual errors, omissions, or misleading statements: 162 in Wikipedia and 123 in Britannica, resulting in an average of 3.86 errors per article for Wikipedia and 2.92 for Britannica. Although Britannica was found to be more accurate, it contested Nature's study as flawed and misleading, arguing that two articles were from a Britannica yearbook and two from Compton's Encyclopedia (listed as the Britannica Student Encyclopedia on the company's website). Nature defended its findings and refused to retract, stating it used whatever relevant material was available on Britannica's website. In a 2009 interview, the managing director of Britannica UK stated that Wikipedia is a fun site with interesting entries, but its approach wouldn't work for Britannica; he described Wikipedia as a chisel and Britannica as a drill, emphasizing the need for the correct tool for the job. For the 15th anniversary of Wikipedia, the Telegraph published opinion pieces falsely claiming that Britannica had gone bankrupt in 1996. In a January 2016 press release, Britannica acknowledged Wikipedia as an impressive achievement but urged critics to avoid false comparisons due to differing models and purposes. Since the 3rd edition, the Britannica has maintained a popular and critical reputation for general excellence, though it has faced criticism. The 3rd and 9th editions were pirated in the United States, beginning with Dobson's Encyclopædia. Upon the release of the 14th edition, Time magazine called the Britannica the "Patriarch of the Library." In a related advertisement, naturalist William Beebe stated that the Britannica was "beyond comparison because there is no competitor." References to the Britannica appear in English literature, notably in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes story "The Red-Headed League," highlighted by the Lord Mayor of London, Gilbert Inglefield, at the Britannica's bicentennial. The Britannica is known for summarizing knowledge; some people have devoted years to reading the entire work, taking between three and 22 years to complete it. When Fat'h Ali became Shah of Persia in 1797, he was given a set of the 3rd edition; after reading it, he extended his title to "Most Formidable Lord and Master of the Encyclopædia Britannica." George Bernard Shaw claimed to have read the complete 9th edition except for science articles; Richard Evelyn Byrd used the Britannica during his five-month stay at the South Pole in 1934; Philip Beaver read it during a sailing expedition. A. J. Jacobs, an editor at Esquire, read the entire 2002 15th edition, documenting his journey in the 2004 book The Know-It-All: One Man's Humble Quest to Become the Smartest Person in the World. Only two people are known to have read two independent editions: author C. S. Forester and Amos Urban Shirk, who read the 11th and 14th editions, spending roughly three hours per night for four and a half years reading the 11th. The CD/DVD-ROM version of the Britannica, Encyclopædia Britannica Ultimate Reference Suite, received the 2004 Distinguished Achievement Award from the Association of Educational Publishers. On 15 July 2009, Encyclopædia Britannica was named one of the "Top Ten Superbrands in the UK" by a panel of over 2,000 independent reviewers, as reported by the BBC. Topics are selected in part based on the Propædia "Outline of Knowledge." The bulk of the 15th edition is devoted to geography (26% of the Macropædia), biography (14%), biology and medicine (11%), literature (7%), physics and astronomy (6%), religion (5%), art (4%), Western philosophy (4%), and law (3%). A complementary study of the Micropædia found that geography accounted for 25% of articles, science 18%, social sciences 17%, biography 17%, and all other humanities 25%. In 1992, a reviewer judged that the "range, depth, and catholicity of coverage [of the Britannica] are unsurpassed by any other general Encyclopaedia." The Britannica does not cover topics equally; for example, the whole of Buddhism and most other religions are covered in a single Macropædia article, while 14 articles are devoted to Christianity, comprising nearly half of all religion articles. The Britannica includes 50,479 biographies, 5,999 of which are about women, with 11.87% British and 25.51% U.S. citizens. It has been praised as the least biased general encyclopedia marketed to Western readers and for its biographies of important women across eras. It can be stated without contradiction that the 15th edition of the Britannica gives non-Western cultural, social, and scientific developments more attention than any other general English-language encyclopedia currently available. Kenneth Kister, in Kister's Best Encyclopedias (1994), made this claim. Harvey Einbinder, in The Myth of the Britannica, criticized the 11th edition for being inaccessible to laymen, noting that many articles were too technical for non-specialists. He made similar criticisms of the mathematics and science articles in the 14th edition. On rare occasions, the Britannica has faced criticism for editorial choices. Given its constant size, the encyclopaedia has had to reduce or eliminate some topics to accommodate others, leading to controversial decisions. The initial 15th edition (1974–1985) was criticized for eliminating coverage of children's literature, military decorations, and the French poet Joachim du Bellay; editorial errors were also alleged, such as inconsistent sorting of Japanese biographies. The elimination of the index and the arbitrary division of articles into the Micropædia and Macropædia were also condemned. One critic described the initial 15th edition as a "qualified failure ... that cares more for juggling its format than for preserving." More recently, American Library Association reviewers were surprised to find that most educational articles had been removed from the 1992 Macropædia, along with the article on psychology. Harvey Einbinder criticized the practice of condensing entries in the 14th edition, which often involved simply removing large amounts of text without rewriting, resulting in a significant reduction in article quality. Some Britannica-appointed contributors have made errors; a notable early instance was George Gleig, chief editor of the 3rd edition (1788–1797), who incorrectly stated that gravity was caused by the classical element of fire. The Britannica has also defended a scientific approach to cultural topics, as seen in William Robertson Smith's articles on religion in the 9th edition, particularly his claim that the Bible was not historically accurate (1875). The Britannica has received criticism, especially as editions become outdated, and it is expensive to produce a completely new edition.

The American Library Association was surprised to discover that most educational articles had been removed from the 1992 Macropædia, along with the article on psychology. Harvey Einbinder, in his 1964 book *The Myth of the Britannica*, criticized the practice of condensing entries in the 14th edition, noting that it typically involved simply deleting large amounts of text rather than rewriting it, which he believed significantly reduced article quality. A notable historical error occurred in the 3rd edition (1788–1797), when chief editor George Gleig incorrectly stated that gravity was caused by the classical element of fire. The Britannica has also maintained a scientific stance on cultural topics, as seen in William Robertson Smith’s 1875 article in the 9th edition, which argued the Bible was not historically accurate. The encyclopaedia has faced criticism, especially as editions grow outdated; producing a complete new edition is costly, and editors often delay updates for about 25 years. The 14th edition, despite continuous revision, became outdated after 35 years (1929–1964), prompting the 15th edition, which took 10 years to produce. Critics have noted that articles, particularly in the Macropædia, are often out-of-date, with longer entries being more likely to be outdated than shorter Micropædia ones, and inconsistencies between Micropædia and Macropædia entries due to uneven updates. The bibliographies in Macropædia articles have also been criticized as being more out-of-date than the articles themselves. In 2005, a 12-year-old British schoolboy identified inaccuracies in entries on Poland and wildlife in Eastern Europe. In 2010, an incorrect description of the Irish Civil War—presented as a conflict between north and south Ireland—was discussed in the Irish press after the Department of Education and Science funded online access. George Gleig, in writing about the 3rd edition, observed that "perfection seems to be incompatible with the nature of works constructed on such a plan and embracing such a variety of subjects." In March 2006, the Britannica stated, "we in no way mean to imply that Britannica is error-free; we have never made such a claim," a sentiment echoed in the introduction to the first edition by William Smellie, who acknowledged that critics could point out more errors than any editor could account for. However, in 1962, the Britannica sales department had claimed that the 14th edition contained "it is truth. It is unquestionable fact." The 14th edition saw annual revisions from 1929 to 1973, except in 1931, 1934, and 1935, and annual revisions continued from 1974 to 2007, except in 1996, 1999, 2000, 2004, and 2006. The 15th edition, introduced as "Britannica 3," consisted of a 10-volume Micropædia, a 19-volume Macropædia, and the Propædia. In 1985, the system was updated with a separate two-volume index, and Macropædia articles were consolidated into fewer, larger entries—such as combining all 50 U.S. state articles into a single "United States of America" article—with some medium-length articles moved to the Micropædia, resulting in a 12-volume Micropædia and a 17-volume Macropædia. The first CD-ROM edition was released in 1994, accompanied by a paid online version; in 1999, the online version became free, and no revised print editions were issued. The online experiment ended in 2001, and a new printed set was released that same year.
